query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In nanoscale FCC/BCC high‐entropy alloy multilayers, sustained loading promotes progressive plastic deformation by triggering localized dislocation generation and pile‐up at the chemically and structurally distinct multilayer interfaces. As the stress is held over time, interfacial regions—characterized by severe lattice distortion and pre‐existing short‐range order—gradually yield by accommodating accumulating dislocations via thermally activated climb and cooperative activation of otherwise dormant slip systems. This interfacial plasticity then locally softens the layers, allowing further strain partitioning throughout the multilayer stack without compromising the overall nanoscale coating architecture.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating composed of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy layers with optimized (moderate negative) lattice misfit and established short-range order, exhibiting low initial dislocation density and high interfacial stability.
generation.intervention: Apply a constant, sustained load (creep test) over extended durations at a controlled temperature that is high enough to activate dislocation climb but below levels causing catastrophic failure.
generation.conditions: Testing should be carried out under isothermal, constant-stress conditions with the multilayer structure retained (nanoscale layer thickness maintained) and with controlled strain rates to balance diffusion-assisted glide and climb.
generation.structural_mediator: The multilayer interfaces, which possess enhanced lattice distortions and altered short-range order relative to the layer interiors, serve as both barriers and stepping stones for dislocation motion, thereby mediating the progression of plastic deformation.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained loading, dislocations nucleate preferentially at the distorted multilayer interfaces. These dislocations initially pile up, locally increasing the stress concentration until a threshold is reached. At that point, thermally activated dislocation climb and cooperative slip are activated, leading to gradual local softening and the onset of homogeneous plastic flow across adjacent layers while still preserving the multilayer architecture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Over time, when stressed under sustained loading, in situ observations and nanoindentation tests will reveal: (1) increasing plastic strain localized mainly at the interfaces, (2) an observable evolution of dislocation density and arrangement (including pile-ups and eventual release into adjacent layers), and (3) a gradual reduction in local hardness at interfacial zones relative to the initial baseline.
generation.baseline: The initial state showing a homogeneous, highly stable multilayered structure with low dislocation density and uniformly high hardness across both FCC and BCC layers.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold when the nanoscale multilayer architecture is preserved (i.e. layer thickness remains on the order of tens to a few hundred nanometers), the applied stresses are moderate (below the immediate onset of catastrophic failure), and the testing temperature is such that diffusion-assisted mechanisms (dislocation climb) are active but not so high as to induce premature softening or phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis extends findings from (PMC12964539::web::022) and (PMC12842692::web::025), which discuss dislocation behavior in HEAs and the role of lattice misfit in creep; here we have extrapolated those observations into a multilayer configuration. Uncertainty remains in quantifying how the interplay between FCC and BCC responses and the chemical short-range order at interfaces specifically modulates dislocation nucleation and release dynamics, which needs direct experimental verification in multilayer systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform an in situ TEM creep experiment on a nanoscale FCC/BCC HEA multilayer coating subjected to a constant load at a controlled temperature. Monitor real-time dislocation activity, dislocation pile-up at interfaces, and local hardness changes using high-resolution imaging and nanoindentation mapping over the course of sustained loading.
measurements: Evolution of dislocation density and arrangement at and near multilayer interfaces
Local strain distribution and onset of interfacial softening
Hardness variations across the multilayer cross-section before, during, and after loading
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiments do not show preferential dislocation accumulation or pile-up at the multilayer interfaces, or if the local softening and progressive plastic deformation occur uniformly across the layers (without interfacial mediation) under sustained load, then the hypothesis is falsified.
